questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was reviewed as part of contact tracing for an acute case of hepatitis A in a childcare center. She worked as a nursery nurse, had been born and brought up in the United States, and had no recent travel. She was asymptomatic. She was usually well and was not taking any regular medications.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Screen for underlying immunodeficiency or liver disorders

questions.explanation: Give single-dose HAV vaccination. Postexposure prophylaxis is warranted as the index case was in a childcare center, caring for children likely to still be in diapers. Food handlers and close household/sexual contacts of a confirmed case would also be advised to receive PEP . For healthy persons aged 12 months to 40 years, single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine at the age-appropriate dose is preferred to immunoglobulin because of the vaccine’s advantages, including long-term protection and ease of administration, as well as the equivalent efficacy of vaccine to immunoglobulin. Adults ≥40 or with immunocompromised or chronic liver disease also required HAV immunoglobulin. For more information, see https://www.cdc.gov/hepatit is/hav/havfaq.htm.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q22

questions.question: A child has clinical hepatitis A. Household contacts have been exposed.
questions.question_raw: HepA exposure to kid with clinical hep A.

parts.text: How do you diagnose hepatitis A?
What do you do with the following contacts: the pregnant mother; a 5-year-old sibling; a 10-month-old sibling?

parts_raw.text: A.  How to diagnose?
B. What do you do with the following contacts? Pregnant mom; Five year old sibling?; 10 month old sibling?

questions.model_answer:
a) Detection of hepatitis A-specific IgM (anti-HAV IgM) in a single acute-phase serum sample; it is usually present at initial evaluation and confirms acute infection. (If negative early but HAV clinically suspected, repeat, since ~10% are initially negative.)
b) Give post-exposure prophylaxis to household contacts as soon as possible (within 14 days): (1) Pregnant mother (healthy adult): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine; pregnancy is not a contraindication (IG is an acceptable alternative). (2) 5-year-old sibling (≥12 mo, healthy): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (3) 10-month-old sibling (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM, not vaccine, because HAV vaccine is not indicated for PEP in infants under 12 months.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives vaccine to all three contacts, but per Table 174.2 the 10-month-old (<12 months) should receive immune globulin, not vaccine.

cohort_answer.text:
Hep A IgM
Vaccine
Vaccine
Vaccine

questions.question: A man returns from India with hepatitis A.
questions.question_raw: Man comes back from India with Hepatitis A.

parts.text: What post-exposure prophylaxis do you provide for his pregnant wife, his 9-month-old, and his 15-month-old? He wants to return to India — does he need hepatitis A vaccine? His sister had one dose 9 years ago and also wants to travel to India — does she need 1 or 2 doses, and why?

parts_raw.text: What PEP do you provide for his pregnant wife, 9 month old, 15 month old. He wants to go back to India, does he need hepatitis A vaccine? His sister has one dose 9 years ago. She wants to go to India too! she need 1 or 2 doses? Why?

questions.model_answer:
Give household-contact PEP as soon as possible (effective within 14 days of exposure): (1) Pregnant wife (healthy adult): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine; pregnancy is not a contraindication. (2) 9-month-old (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM — vaccine is not used for PEP under 12 months. (3) 15-month-old (≥12 mo, healthy): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine.
Return to India: No vaccine needed — natural HAV infection confers lifelong immunity; second attacks are not documented.
Sister (one dose 9 years ago): only 1 additional (second) dose is required, not a restart of the series. The first dose does not need to be repeated regardless of the interval; the series is simply completed, and a robust anamnestic response is expected.

questions.question: Name six people or groups who should receive pre-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis A.

parts.text: Name six people or groups of people to give pre-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis A.

parts_raw.text: Name 6 people or groups of people to give pre-exposure prophylaxis for Hep A

questions.model_answer: (1) International travelers to or workers in high- or intermediate-endemicity countries. (2) Men who have sex with men. (3) People who use injection and non-injection illicit drugs. (4) Persons with chronic liver disease. (5) Persons who receive clotting factor concentrates. (6) Persons anticipating close contact with an international adoptee from a high/intermediate-endemicity country. (Also acceptable: all children 12–23 months; persons who work with HAV in research or with nonhuman primates; anyone wishing to obtain immunity.)

parts.text: How do you diagnose it?

parts_raw.text: How do you diagnose
What prophylaxis for family members (mother, 5 y.o brother, 10 months old sister)

questions.model_answer:
a) Detection of hepatitis A-specific IgM (anti-HAV IgM) in a single acute-phase serum sample confirms acute hepatitis A.
b) Post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible (within 14 days): (1) Mother (healthy adult): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (2) 5-year-old brother (≥12 mo): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (3) 10-month-old sister (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM — vaccine is not used for PEP under 12 months. Immunocompromised contacts or those with chronic liver disease should receive both vaccine and IG.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort vaccinates all family members, but per Table 174.2 the 10-month-old (<12 months) should receive immune globulin rather than vaccine.

cohort_answer.text: How do you diagnose: Serum antibody (IgM). Prophylaxis for family members: Vaccination for all of them; And IVIG if any of them are immunocompromised

questions.question: Hepatitis A vaccination as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

parts.text: Give 6 populations / patient groups who should have Hepatitis A vaccination as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

parts_raw.text: Give 6 populations / patient groups who should have Hepatitis A vaccination as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Travellers to or workers in countries with endemic hepatitis A. (2) Men who have sex with men. (3) People who use injection or non-injection illicit drugs. (4) Persons with chronic liver disease (including chronic HBV/HCV) or awaiting/after liver transplant. (5) Persons with haemophilia or receiving repeated plasma-derived clotting factor concentrates. (6) Household members/close contacts and caregivers of adoptees from endemic countries; also zoo/veterinary/laboratory workers handling HAV or non-human primates, residents and staff of facilities for the developmentally disabled, some Indigenous and other communities with recurrent outbreaks, and people experiencing homelessness or incarceration.

questions.question: A man returns from a trip to India with symptoms concerning for hepatitis A virus infection. Scenarios involving post-exposure prophylaxis for HAV.
questions.question_raw: Scenarios involving PEP For HAV. Man comes back from trip in India with symptoms concerning for HAV.

parts.text: What is the single best test to confirm the diagnosis?
Assuming the diagnosis is confirmed, what do you do for each of the following individuals: adult wife, 5-year-old child, 9-month-old child?
The patient recovers and is planning a trip back to India 6 months later. He asks whether he still needs to be vaccinated. What do you tell him?
A woman who received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive 1 or 2 doses this time. What do you tell her and why?
What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the single best test to confirm dx?
B) Assuming diagnosis confirmed, what do you do for each of the following individuals: Adult wife, 5 year old child, 9 month old child
C) The patient recovers, and is now planning a trip back to India 6 months later. He asks whether he still needs to be vaccinated. What do you tell him?

D) A woman who has received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive 1 or 2 doses of vaccine this time around. What do you tell her and why?
E) What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

questions.model_answer:
a) Hepatitis A-specific IgM (anti-HAV IgM) in a single acute-phase serum sample.
b) Household-contact PEP within 14 days: (1) Adult wife (healthy): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (2) 5-year-old (≥12 mo): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (3) 9-month-old (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM — vaccine is not used for PEP under 12 months.
c) No vaccine needed — natural infection confers lifelong immunity; reinfection does not occur. (Advise hepatitis B vaccination if not already immune.)
d) Only 1 additional (second) dose is needed; the first dose is not repeated regardless of the 9-year interval. An anamnestic response occurs and the two-dose series simply completes for long-term protection.
e) Inactivated single-antigen vaccines, two-dose series: Havrix (peds 720 ELU / adult 1440 ELU) at 0 and 6–12 months; VAQTA (peds 25 U / adult 50 U) at 0 and 6–18 months. Combination Twinrix (≥18 yr): 3 doses at 0, 1, 6 months. Immune globulin for PEP: 0.1 mL/kg IM.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort vaccinates the 9-month-old within 14 days, but per Table 174.2 an infant under 12 months should receive immune globulin, not vaccine.

cohort_answer.text:
Hepatitis A IgM (gold standard, + at 5-10 days, remains + for 3-12 months)
Adult wife - vaccinate within 14 days (if <60 years); 5 year old child - vaccinate within 14 days; 9 month old child - vaccinate within 14 days
Patients who acquire HAV (naturally or via vaccine) are immune for life, cannot get HAV twice. Advise Hep B vaccine if not already vaccinated
One dose of monovalent HA vaccine given for primary immunization with booster dose at least 6-36 months later for lifelong protection; she only needs one additional dose
2 doses: 0 and 6 months

questions.model_answer:
a) Hepatitis A-specific IgM (anti-HAV IgM) in a single acute-phase serum sample.
b) Household-contact PEP within 14 days: (1) Adult wife (healthy): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine (complete series with a second dose ≥6 months later for long-term immunity). (2) 5-year-old (≥12 mo): single dose of hepatitis A vaccine. (3) 9-month-old (<12 mo): immune globulin 0.1 mL/kg IM — vaccine is not indicated for PEP under 12 months.
c) No vaccine needed — natural HAV infection confers lifelong immunity.
d) Only 1 additional dose is required; the earlier dose counts and the series is completed rather than restarted, with a rapid anamnestic response.

cohort_answer.text: A) Hepatitis A IgM. B) Adult wife: vaccinate with 1 dose of hep A vaccine if no prior vaccination hx, second dose at 6 months, ideally within 14 days but ASAP preferred. 5 year old child: vaccinate. 9 month old child: vaccinate; immunoglobulin indicated in 0-12 month age group but vaccination preferred if >6 months. C) Natural infection confers lifelong immunity for HAV; no need for vaccine.

questions.question: A woman who received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip.
questions.question_raw: Q49. A woman who has received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive one or two doses of vaccine this time around.

parts.text: What do you tell her and why, and what are the dosage schedules for HAV?

parts_raw.text: What do you tell her and why? What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

questions.model_answer:
She needs only 1 additional (second) dose, not a restart of the series — the first dose is not repeated regardless of the 9-year interval, and an anamnestic response provides long-term (estimated 20–30 year) protection once the series is complete.
Dosage schedules: two-dose inactivated single-antigen vaccine — Havrix (720 ELU peds / 1440 ELU adult) at 0 and 6–12 months; VAQTA (25 U peds / 50 U adult) at 0 and 6–18 months; combination Twinrix (≥18 yr) at 0, 1, 6 months.

cohort_answer.text: Only 1 additional dose of HAV vaccine needed. Usual dosing at 0 and 6-36 months.

questions.question_raw: For the following organisms, list the latest time that Ig can be given as PEP.

parts.text: Measles
Varicella-zoster virus
Hepatitis B

parts_raw.text: Measles
VZV

questions.model_answer: a) Measles: within 6 days of exposure (active vaccine if given within 72 hours). b) VZV: as soon as possible, up to 10 days after exposure. c) Hepatitis B: as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and up to 7 days after percutaneous/perinatal exposure (up to 14 days after sexual exposure). d) Hepatitis A: within 2 weeks (14 days) of exposure. e) Rabies: RIG given with the first vaccine dose; if not given then, it can still be administered through day 7 of the vaccine series.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rabies figure (RIG through day 7) is from this chapter; the measles, VZV, hepatitis B and hepatitis A immunoglobulin windows are from CDC/ACIP and PHAC immunization guidance, not the Mandell rabies chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Measles: 6 days (vaccine within 72 hrs). VZV: 96 hours – 10 days. Hepatitis B: 12 hours, up to 7 days for needle and infants, 14 days for sexual contact. Hepatitis A: 14 days. Rabies: up to Day 7 after vaccine given.

questions.question: You see a patient with severe sepsis. He recently traveled to Florida where he consumed many raw oysters.
questions.question_raw: You see a patient with severe sepsis. He recently traveled to Florida where he consumed many raw oysters.

parts.text: What is the most likely bacteria causing his infection?
List THREE clinical syndromes associated with this bacteria.
List THREE risk factors for severe sepsis with this bacteria.
List TWO common viral infections that are associated with eating raw oysters.

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely bacteria causing his infection?
List THREE clinical syndromes associated with this bacteria.
List THREE risk factors for severe sepsis with this bacteria.
List TWO common viral infections that are associated with eating raw oysters.

questions.model_answer:
a) Vibrio vulnificus.
b) (1) Primary septicemia (abrupt chills/fever, hypotension, metastatic hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions) following raw-oyster ingestion (2) Rapidly progressive necrotizing wound infection/cellulitis after seawater exposure (3) Acute self-limited diarrheal illness.
c) (1) Cirrhosis/underlying liver disease (2) Iron-overload states (hemochromatosis, hemolytic anemia, chronic renal failure) (3) Malignancy, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medications.
d) (1) Norovirus (2) Hepatitis A virus.
questions.beyond_mandell: The two oyster-associated viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A) are established general knowledge, not from this chapter.
